blocks.text: 我们在把 Messages API 从 Python 迁移到 Rust 时就遇到了这个问题。这个 API 是客户以及我们自己的应用（比如 Claude Code 和 Cowork）访问 Claude 的主要途径。从 2024 年初到 2026 年秋，API 流量增长了约 1,800 倍。改用 Rust 后，每个请求消耗的 CPU 会少得多。Claude 用大约一周时间写出了这个 API 核心请求路径的第一版。但要让人信任这次迁移，我们必须找到一种办法，验证 Rust 版 API 与生产环境 API 行为一致。这件事之所以困难，原因有好几个：Python 版 API 在整个迁移过程中一直在变，所以“一致”是个不断移动的目标；Claude 对同一个请求的回复可能不确定，所以两份输出有差异不一定就是 bug；而且我们看不到客户的请求内容，也就无法轻易发现两个版本在哪里出现了分歧。

blocks.text: 为什么要迁移？

inlines.text: 为什么要迁移？

blocks.text: 我们在 2023 年构建了 Messages API，用 Python 编写，因为当时公司内部大量研究代码都用 Python。起初它很简单：Messages API 把请求转给模型，再把模型写出的内容发回去。（当时有位工程师称它“基本就是个请求转发器”。）但随着 Messages API 功能越来越强、与我们的代码库结合得越来越深，它也开始与研究团队和推理团队维护的 Python 库产生共享依赖，这让它很难挪动。如果哪天想换用另一种语言，就意味着日志、指标和工具全都要重新做一遍。

blocks.text: 要验证迁移，首先需要定义什么叫“正确”。有几种做法（图 3）。运气好的话，你可以直接写一条规则。数学中的定理就是一个精确的陈述，证明助手（比如 Lean）可以依据一套固定规则检查证明的每一步。另一些时候——在软件工程中更常见——你用一组示例来定义“正确”，比如测试。例如，Bun 从 Zig 迁移到 Rust 时，它的测试套件是用 TypeScript 写的，因此同一套测试可以评判两个版本。在我们的案例中，这两种方法都不够用，于是我们以现有系统作为基准，在迁移过程中测试两者是否一致。但问题在于，我们的现有系统（Messages API）一直在变。我们定期发布新模型、上线新功能，这让“正确”的定义成了一个移动靶。

blocks.text: 测试与 Python 实现耦合在一起。一个集成测试会发送请求，然后检查返回结果以及发送给其他服务的内容。我们的测试在测试进程内运行 Python API，并在 Python 内存中模拟计费、限流等服务。测试必须随代码一起改动，而 Claude 在两方面都帮了忙。这样一来，一个“通过”可能意味着代码是对的，也可能意味着测试被改成了能让错误代码通过的样子。我们确实看到了这种情况：审计移植后的测试时，发现了 100 多处被弱化的断言。

一旦大致知道每处差异位于哪里，我们还需要一种方法来区分不同的 bug。我们记录每处差异在提示词中的起始位置，以及两个版本之间的长度差。结合检查点定位到的步骤和提示词片段，我们发现 bug 会呈现出特定的指纹。也就是说，同一个 bug 往往会在它影响的每个请求上留下相同的指纹（图 9）。这样我们就能按指纹对错误分组，有助于安排修复的优先级。

blocks.text: 主要的限制在于，智能体只能看到指纹，看不到每条记录背后的请求。于是智能体会先假设差异的成因，然后自己写一个请求或模型回复，试图复现这个差异。由于这些内容都是智能体自己写的，它可以完整读取两边的结果。如果结果一致，说明它的猜测错了，智能体会再试一次。如果结果以记录所描述的方式出现差异，智能体就会修改 Rust，直到两个版本一致，然后补一个在旧代码上失败、在新代码上通过的测试（图 11）。

blocks.text: Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work.

blocks.text: We ran into this problem when we migrated our Messages API from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. But building trust in the migration required us to find a way to verify that our Rust API was at parity with our production API. This proved hard for several reasons, including that the Python API continued changing throughout the migration, so parity was a moving target; Claude can reply nondeterministically to the same request, so a difference between two outputs didn’t necessarily mean a bug; and we couldn't read customer requests, so we weren't able to easily see where the two versions diverged.

blocks.text: In this post, we share how we turned the production Messages API itself into a verifier—and how that helped us test the new Rust version on production traffic, find where it differed, and automatically dispatch agents to fix those differences. blocks.text: We built the Messages API in 2023 and wrote it in Python, which was widely used internally for much of our research code. At first, it was simple. The Messages API passed requests to the model and sent back what the model wrote. (One engineer at the time called it “basically a request forwarder.”) But as the Messages API became more capable and deeply integrated with our codebases, it also developed shared dependencies with Python libraries that were owned by our research and inference teams, which made it hard to move. If we ever wanted to move to another language, it would mean building logging, metrics, and tools all over again.

blocks.text: To verify the migration, we first needed to define what “correct” meant. You can do this in a few ways (Figure 3). If you’re lucky, you can simply write a rule. A theorem in mathematics is a precise statement, and a proof assistant (like Lean) can check each step of a proof against a fixed set of rules. Other times—and more frequently in software engineering—you define “correct” with a set of examples, like tests. For instance, when Bun moved from Zig to Rust, its test suite was written in TypeScript, so the same tests could judge both versions. In our case, neither approach was sufficient, so we used the existing system as an oracle to test parity during the migration. In this case, our existing system (the Messages API) kept changing. We were releasing new models and shipping new features regularly, which made the definition of “correct” a moving target.

blocks.text: Production data is sometimes “the only true test” that new code behaves like the old code. Running requests through old and new code and comparing the results is often called shadowing. To understand what we needed to compare, it helps to walk through what happens to a single request on the Messages API (Figure 5). The API validates each request, converts it into a prompt a model can read (the prompt for inference), tokenizes it, and runs it through safety classifiers. A model then writes a reply, one token at a time. On the output side, the API sorts those tokens into text, thinking, and tool calls, streams them to the customer, and counts usage for limits and billing.

blocks.text: Our Rust API passed about 98% of its tests in April, yet only about a quarter of inputs matched on production traffic (Figure 6). Checkpointing.

Both API versions handle a request using the same steps: accept or reject it, resolve its settings, build the prompt. Every step produces some result, such as an error or the pieces of the prompt, that we could compare step by step, and within the prompt, piece by piece. The first place they differed indicated roughly where the migration code differed from production code (Figure 8).

Fingerprint.

Once we knew roughly where each diff resided, we still needed a way to distinguish one bug from another. We recorded where each difference began in the prompt, as well as the length difference between the two versions. Combined with the step and piece of the prompt isolated in checkpointing, we found that bugs presented with a specific fingerprint. That is, one bug tends to leave the same fingerprint on every request it affects (Figure 9). We could then group errors by fingerprint, which helped us triage the fixes.

blocks.text: Looking ahead

inlines.text: Looking ahead

blocks.text: It’s increasingly feasible to migrate production systems with Claude, either for better performance or security, without taking an API offline or slowing feature development. Now that the hard part is no longer writing new code, we need to build sufficient confidence that the new system behaves like the old one.

inlines.text: It’s increasingly feasible to migrate production systems with Claude, either for better performance or security, without taking an API offline or slowing feature development. Now that the hard part is no longer writing new code, we need to build sufficient confidence that the new system behaves like the old one.

blocks.text: The usual approach to migration is a bit like rebuilding the Ship of Theseus, in which the old ship was replaced plank by plank. Generally it’s been possible to replace planks while the ship still sails, but changing too many planks at once requires coming into dock. To fully stretch the metaphor, Claude now makes it possible to build an identically functioning ship alongside the first—even as the first keeps sailing and having its planks replaced. Agents kept the new ship in step as the old one changed, and we kept checking that the two behaved the same. Once we trusted that they did, we moved the passengers over a few at a time. The new ship sails faster and more efficiently than the old one.

blocks.text: Lessons learned

inlines.text: Lessons learned

blocks.text: Verification is the new bottleneck. Previously, large software projects like migrations were hard to justify because they took too much effort and carried too much risk. But if writing code is no longer the bottleneck, the main constraint becomes how quickly you can verify results. In general, ambition can be increased as long as there’s a way for Claude to verify correctness.

blocks.text: Verification is how you earn confidence. In math, we use a proof assistant to verify that each step of a proof Claude wrote is valid. For software, tests or formal verification can help us gain similar confidence. But when these checks aren’t enough, a production system itself can also be a verifier.

blocks.text: Carefully design the verification signal. A verifier provides a signal that Claude can act on. We can calibrate this signal to show Claude where things went wrong. Where a proof assistant points to the failing step or a test names the failing case, a production system often offers no such signal by default. Much of our effort for this project went to building such a signal. In this case, checkpoints located each difference in the code and fingerprints helped tell one bug from another.

blocks.text: Build loops that let Claude autonomously act on the signal. Our inner loop was fast and ran locally in a sandbox. Agents tested hypotheses in seconds using requests they wrote themselves. The outer loop was slower and checked fixes on shadowed production traffic. The outermost loop was just prose, with corrections saved as rules in memory that could be read by every agent later in the process. Together, these loops allowed us to migrate the Messages API to Rust, which uses about 70% less CPU per request and reduces median time to first token by about 20% (Figure 15).

blocks.text: Move toward outer loops. At first, we had our engineers working inside the inner loop, running Claude and chasing differences themselves. Later, they moved to the seam between loops, helping to steer agents and reviewing fixes in Slack. But as the system matured, they increasingly moved to the edge, where they could provide the highest leverage, writing the rules and checks that agents worked within. As Claude grew more intelligent (and as we grew more intelligent at working with it), we evolved from directing Claude to Claude directing itself, relying on humans mainly for important judgment calls.
